candidates.title: Use some, but not excessive, best-of-n at fixed inference budget
candidates.rule: When trading model size against reranking samples under a fixed inference-compute budget, use a moderate amount of rejection sampling (e.g. best-of-4 to best-of-64 scaling with model size) rather than pushing n as high as possible.
candidates.passage: We found that it is generally compute-efficient to use some amount of rejection sampling, but not too much.
candidates.finding: Sweeping policy/reward-model size against n, the Pareto-efficient points were 760M best-of-4, 13B best-of-16, 175B best-of-64. Performance was scored with a separate 175B validation reward model, which tracked human preference well for n up to 64; the authors expect it to overestimate preference at larger n due to overoptimization.
workloads: ELI5 long-form question answering with web browsing
candidates.conditions: Policy and reward model scaled together; validation reward model held out on a separate data split; n in {4,16,64}.
candidates.limitations: Compute-efficiency frontier is specific to these model sizes, this reward model quality and this task; the metric is a reward-model proxy, not human judgment, for most points; larger n was not validated against humans.
candidates.validation_test: Plot task score against total inference FLOPs for several model sizes crossed with n, using a held-out reward model plus a human spot-check, and confirm the Pareto frontier shape in your setting.

reason: The paper runs matched comparisons between rejection sampling (best-of-n) against a reward model, RL (PPO), and behavior cloning for a browsing QA agent, and reports compute-efficiency trade-offs; these support narrowly scoped rules about preference optimization choices. A second rule about requiring quoted references to make human evaluation of factual accuracy feasible is supported but less directly measured, so framed as inferred with the agreement-rate and TruthfulQA evidence noted.
